analysis.one_liner: Lets judges ignore federal agencies' interpretations of the laws they enforce.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how courts review federal agency decisions. Today, courts generally give weight to an agency's own reading of the laws it administers (the doctrine known as Chevron deference). This bill would require judges to decide questions of law from scratch instead, with no deference to the agency. It would apply to every legal challenge to any agency action, including rules on pollution, workplace safety, health care, and finance, and no other law could opt out of this standard unless it named this section specifically.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and other regulated parties that challenge federal rules in court. Without deference to agencies, judges would be far more likely to side with challengers and strike down or reinterpret rules on the environment, workplace safety, consumer finance, and health care. Conservative legal groups and industry litigants have long sought this change.

how_it_helps.text: Requires courts reviewing agency actions to decide 'de novo' all questions of law, including the meaning of statutes and agency rules, removing the weight courts currently give an agency's own interpretation.

Applies this no-deference standard to every action for judicial review of agency action under any law, and bars other statutes from exempting cases from it unless they specifically reference this section.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal agencies to enforce protections: cleaner air and water, safer workplaces, safer drugs and food, and fair financial practices would all become easier to challenge and overturn in court. Agencies would also have a harder time carrying out laws Congress wrote in broad terms, since their reasonable interpretations would no longer carry weight.

drawbacks.text: Federal rules on pollution, safety, and consumer protection would be easier for regulated companies to overturn, because a judge with no agency expertise could simply substitute a different reading of the law.

The change would invite a surge of litigation over every contested rule, injecting years of uncertainty into programs people depend on, and would shift power from expert agencies to generalist judges.

Supporters argue the bill restores the Constitution's design by returning questions of law to courts rather than the executive branch; an honest supporter must acknowledge that the cost is less stable, more litigable regulation across the board.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine constitutional argument that judges, not agencies, should decide what the law means. But the practical effect falls mostly in one direction: rules that constrain businesses become harder to defend, and the people those rules protect bear the cost in weaker enforcement and prolonged uncertainty. The bill's blanket application to every agency action, with no carve-outs, would reach far beyond contested cases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the entire Congress; it was sent to a subcommittee in November 2022 and never received a markup or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Scott Fitzgerald introduced the bill on May 25, 2021, with five original Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill attracted 27 cosponsors, all Republicans.

On November 1, 2022, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law — its only action beyond the initial referral — and it never advanced to a committee markup or the House floor.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system of judicial deference to federal agencies remained in place, so agencies and the people who depend on their protections kept the status quo. Businesses hoping to challenge federal rules more easily gained nothing, but nothing was lost either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and people relying on federal rules

for.name: Rep. Scott Fitzgerald
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end judicial deference to agency interpretations of law.

for.name: 27 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action beyond sending it to a subcommittee; never scheduled a markup or vote in the bill's 19 months in committee.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: As chair, never brought the bill to a committee markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill received no committee or floor action, so no roll-call vote exists to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would make every federal rule easier to challenge and overturn in court, since judges would no longer defer to the agency's reading of its own authority. The industry's gain — weaker regulatory enforcement — comes at the cost of the protections ordinary people rely on.
Agencies would lose the judicial weight given to their interpretations of the statutes they administer, making it harder to implement and defend the programs Congress assigns them.
